title: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node. If there are two middle nodes, return the second one. Solve it in a single pass. (LeetCode: Middle of the Linked List)
shortTitle: Middle of the LinkedList (Fast and Slow Pointers)
keyPoints: Use two pointers: slow moves one node per step, fast moves two nodes per step
When fast reaches the end (null or fast.next is null), slow is at the middle
For even-length lists, this returns the second of the two middle nodes
Loop condition while (fast != null && fast.next != null) determines first vs second middle
Single pass with O(n) time and O(1) space, no need to count nodes first
This pattern is a building block for palindrome check, list reordering, and merge sort on lists

s1_definition.oneliner: Fast moves two, slow moves one; when fast hits the end, slow is the middle.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Fast-slow pointers** use two pointers that start at the head and advance at different speeds.
- **Speed ratio** of 2:1 means when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer has covered exactly half the distance.
- **Even-length lists** have two middle candidates; the standard loop condition returns the second middle node.
- **Single pass** means you never need to count the total nodes first, unlike the two-pass approach.
- **Constant space** uses only two pointer variables regardless of list length.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a chain of linked statement pages and wants the middle page without first counting how many pages there are. He sends a slow walker that steps one page at a time and a fast walker that steps two pages at a time. By the time the fast walker reaches the last page, the slow walker is standing exactly on the middle page. No counting, no second trip through the chain.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  List:  P1 → P2 → P3 → P4 → P5

  Step 0: slow=P1  fast=P1
  Step 1: slow=P2  fast=P3
  Step 2: slow=P3  fast=P5
          fast.next = null → stop

  Answer: slow = P3 (middle)
```

```text
  Even-Length List:  P1 → P2 → P3 → P4

  Step 0: slow=P1  fast=P1
  Step 1: slow=P2  fast=P3
  Step 2: slow=P3  fast=null (past P4)
          fast.next would be null → stop at step 1 check
          Actually: fast=P3, fast.next=P4, fast.next.next=null
          So: step 2 executes, slow=P3, fast=P4.next=null
          Loop condition fails → stop

  Answer: slow = P3 (second middle)
```

```text
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Fast-Slow Pointer Pattern           │
  │                                      │
  │  slow ─→ one step at a time          │
  │  fast ─→ two steps at a time         │
  │                                      │
  │  When fast finishes:                 │
  │    distance(fast) = 2 * distance(slow)│
  │    slow is at the midpoint           │
  │                                      │
  │  Applications:                       │
  │    ├── Middle node                   │
  │    ├── Palindrome check              │
  │    ├── List reorder                  │
  │    ├── Merge sort split              │
  │    └── Cycle detection               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the middle node of a singly linked list is the classic fast-slow pointer problem. You start a slow pointer and a fast pointer at the head, and on each step you move slow forward one node and fast forward two nodes. Because fast covers twice the distance, when fast reaches the end, slow has covered exactly half and sits on the middle node.

The loop condition `while (fast != null && fast.next != null)` is what determines behavior on even-length lists. With this condition, you get the second of the two middle nodes. Changing the condition to `while (fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null)` gives the first middle instead. Interviewers often probe this specific detail, so stating your convention explicitly matters.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in a statement viewer that linked a customer's monthly statement pages into a chain. A feature needed to jump straight to the middle page to show a summary split point. Counting all the pages and then walking again was two passes over a potentially long chain, which hurt latency, so the single-pass fast-slow technique gave the middle directly.

The senior-level insight is that this midpoint finder is a foundational building block. It is the first step in checking whether a list is a palindrome, in reordering a list by interleaving from both ends, and in merge sort on linked lists. Mastering this clean single-pass technique pays off across an entire family of linked list problems.

Remember one sentence: slow moves one, fast moves two, and when fast finishes, slow is at the middle.
